newsitem.title: USA: U.S. set to chide Europe, Japan on economic growth.
newsitem.headline: U.S. set to chide Europe, Japan on economic growth.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
The United States is expected to chide Europe and Japan about the need to nurture their fledgling economic recoveries at a meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations on Saturday.
But the criticism is likely to be muted because the outlook for the world economy as a whole looks bright.

"Obviously it will be important to keep the momentum of growth in place in both Europe and Japan," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said. "We'll be looking forward to a frank discussion on these issues."
Faster growth in Europe and Japan would be good for the United States because it would boost demand for American exports, helping sustain its 5-1/2-year-old economic upswing.
For its part, the United States is likely to be faced with questions at the G7 meeting about its willingness to take tough action to balance its government budget and hold inflation in check.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) this week said the United States needs to raise interest rates to prevent the economy from overheating and head off inflation.

Saturday's meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- is shaping up to be a low-key gathering free of the rancour evident in the past.

With the United States and Japan both faced with upcoming elections and Europe preoccupied with its efforts to launch a single currency in 1999, there is little incentive for any of the policymakers to engage in a public war of words.

Currency markets, often the bugaboo of G7 meetings, have remained calm. The dollar has been buoyant, but so far the United States does not seem concerned that will hurt its exporters by robbing them of competitiveness on world markets,
"The key currencies are now in ... a solid, well-justified constellation and we don't forsee major changes in the near future," International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said.
On the one issue that may have sparked heated debate at the G7 meeting -- a controversial proposal to sell IMF gold -- the group has agreed to disagree and put off a decision.
A German source, who declined to be named, said he did not expect open conflict on the issue here in Washington.
The United States and Britain back gold sales to help the world's poor. Germany and Italy are opposed.
The G7 gathering, which is taking place on the fringes of the semi-annual IMF/World Bank meeting, comes as the outlook for the world economy is turning brighter.
The IMF has forecast that world growth will pick up to 4.1 percent next year from 3.8 percent in 1996.
U.S. Treasury Seceratry Robert Rubin has called the global outlook "encouraging" but has also made clear that Washington will be monitoring developments in Europe and Japan closely.
Rubin in the past has raised questions about Europe's head-long drive to slash budget deficits under its plan to launch European Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.

At the last meeting of G7 economic policymakers in April, European nations argued that a stronger dolar was needed to help put their economies back on track, while the United States advocated European interest rate cuts as the solution.
Both have occurred, taking the sting out of the short-term economic debate, but leaving open the question of the long-term impact of EMU on the world economy.
"It (the dollar) is not an issue. We will not be making it an issue," the German source said.
Japanese officials too have signalled that they do not intend to push for a stronger dolar at the G7 meeting.
"The current dollar/yen rate correctly reflects economic fundamentals and I think it is in a comfortable range for both Japan and the United States," a Japanese official said.
Rubin though said that it was "critically important" that Japan continue to pursue policies aimed at promoting domestic demand-led growth.
